questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman attended for review after a positive pregnancy test. She was known to have HIV and was taking tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine/efavirenz. She reported ongoing compliance with her medication. She estimated that she was 7 weeks pregnant. Investigations: CD4 count 550 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Advise her to consider termination due to the risk of teratogenicity
Continue current ART and routine monitoring
Stop ART and recommence during the 2nd trimester
Switch to ritonavir-boosted darunavir, zidovudine, and emtricitabine

questions.explanation: Continue current ART and routine monitoring HIV-infected pregnant women established on ART who present for care during the 1st trimester should continue treatment during pregnancy, provided the regimen is tolerated and effective in suppressing viral replication. Women who become pregnant on efavirenz-containing regimens who are virally suppressed and tolerating it should continue their current regimens. In the past efavirenz was linked with teratogenicity based on animal studies; however, increased teratogenicity has not been seen in the babies of mothers exposed to efavirenz in the 1st trimester in registry studies and meta-analyses. Therefore guidelines recommend continuing treatment: http://aidsinfo.nih.gov/contentfiles/lvgu idelines/PerinatalGL.pd. There is no data on cobicistat in pregnancy, therefore for present protease inhibitors should be ritonavir-boosted.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q34

questions.question: 34yo F, refugee from SS Africa, recently moved to Canada and is 36 weeks pregnant. Screening HIV test positive. Viral load is 77,000 copies/mL, CD4 count is 210. Otherwise healthy. Awaiting genotype and HLAB5701 testing.

parts.text: Give three appropriate ART regimens and when you would start each
Give the regimen for intrapartum ART therapy and mode of delivery
VL of mother at time of delivery is 2700 copies/mL. What is your regimen for the baby and what is the duration of each component.
What is ONE test you need to do in immediate post-partum period and give timing
What is your advice regarding breastfeeding and give TWO reasons

questions.model_answer: a) Three regimens, start immediately: (1) Dolutegravir + TDF/FTC (or TAF/FTC). (2) Raltegravir + TDF/FTC. (3) Ritonavir-boosted atazanavir or darunavir + TDF/FTC. b) Intrapartum: continue oral ART; VL 77,000 unless suppressed by delivery, add IV zidovudine infusion and perform scheduled cesarean section (VL >1000 near term). c) Neonate (maternal VL 2700 at delivery): combination infant ART prophylaxis (zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir) for 4-6 weeks (not AZT monotherapy) given detectable VL >50-1000. d) HIV DNA/RNA PCR at birth, 1-2 months, and 4-6 months. e) Formula feeding recommended in Canada to eliminate residual transmission risk.

questions.question: HIV in Pregnancy at 16 weeks gestation. VL 77K, CD4 210. HLA and resistance testing is pending.

parts.text: Name 3 first line agents to start, and when?
What to give peripartum (VL is 2100)
What is your recommended delivery method?
What HIV diagnostic test is required for the neonate and how soon?
How do you treat the baby and for how long
What is your recommendation for infant feeding and 2 reasons why

questions.model_answer: a) Three first-line agents/regimens: dolutegravir, raltegravir, or ritonavir-boosted darunavir/atazanavir, each combined with TDF/FTC (or TAF/FTC) - start immediately regardless of gestational age. b) Peripartum (VL 2100, i.e. >50-1000): continue oral ART; add IV zidovudine infusion intrapartum given VL not fully suppressed. c) Delivery: scheduled cesarean section recommended (VL >1000 near delivery threshold, or per obstetric risk-benefit if borderline); if VL <1000 at delivery vaginal delivery reasonable. d) Neonatal HIV DNA/RNA PCR testing at birth, then 1-2 months, then 4-6 months. e) Combination infant ART prophylaxis (zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir) for 4-6 weeks given detectable maternal VL. f) Formula feeding recommended in Canada: (1) eliminates residual risk of postnatal transmission via breastmilk, (2) access to safe clean water/formula makes replacement feeding feasible and safer than in resource-limited settings.

questions.question: New diagnosis HIV in pregnant woman from Africa at 36 weeks gestation. Viral load 78k, resistance testing and HLA-B*5701 pending.

parts.text: What are three art regimens to start, and when would you start each?
She has a stat viral load at delivery showing viral load 2700. What management do you recommend for her delivery?
The baby is born. What regimen do you prescribe for baby and for how long?
What is Canada’s recommendation regarding infant feeding? Give two reasons why.

questions.model_answer:
a) Three ART regimens and timing: (1) Dolutegravir + tenofovir/emtricitabine (or lamivudine) - preferred, start immediately/as soon as possible given high viral load and late gestation, no need to await resistance/HLA results (avoid abacavir until HLA-B*5701 negative); (2) Raltegravir-based regimen with tenofovir/emtricitabine - alternative if DTG unavailable/contraindicated, start immediately; (3) Boosted darunavir/ritonavir + tenofovir/emtricitabine - alternative PI-based option, also start immediately given proximity to delivery and high viral load, as PI regimens have long safety track record in pregnancy.
b) Delivery management with VL 2700 near term: recommend intravenous zidovudine intrapartum (VL >1000 copies/mL near delivery) and scheduled Cesarean section at 38 weeks to reduce risk of perinatal transmission.
c) Infant regimen: given maternal viraemia at delivery, infant is at increased transmission risk - give infant combination ART prophylaxis (e.g., zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir/nevirapine) for 6 weeks rather than zidovudine monotherapy.
d) Canada's recommendation on infant feeding: formula feeding (replacement feeding) is recommended rather than breastfeeding when the mother's viral load is not confirmed suppressed. Two reasons: (1) risk of postnatal HIV transmission through breast milk even with maternal ART, particularly with detectable/unknown viral load near delivery; (2) safe, affordable replacement feeding (formula) is readily available in Canada, removing the rationale for accepting transmission risk that exists in resource-limited settings.
questions.beyond_mandell: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC)/Canadian Perinatal HIV guidelines for intrapartum management and infant prophylaxis.

questions.question: You have a mother in clinic who is 38-weeks pregnant who is otherwise healthy. She has been on Biktarvy for her entire pregnancy and is virologically suppressed. She is interested in breastfeeding.

parts.text: Based on the Canadian Pediatric & Perinatal HIV/AIDS Research group consensus recommendations for infant feeding in HIV, what are THREE criteria to proceed with breast feeding?

questions.model_answer: Three criteria per Canadian Perinatal HIV/AIDS Research group consensus to proceed with breastfeeding: (1) maternal HIV RNA suppressed (<50 copies/mL) throughout pregnancy and confirmed near delivery/postpartum; (2) mother is engaged in ongoing HIV care and committed to strict ART adherence, with close monitoring of maternal and infant HIV status throughout breastfeeding; (3) informed, shared decision-making has occurred with counselling on the residual (very low but not zero) risk of transmission, and infant receives appropriate postnatal ARV prophylaxis with regular follow-up testing.
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian Paediatric & Perinatal AIDS Research Group (CPARG) consensus statement on infant feeding in the context of maternal HIV.

questions.question: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care

parts.text: What is baby's risk of acquiring HIV?

cohort_answer.text: 25-40% without ARVs; 1-2% with ARVs

questions.question: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care

parts.text: List 4 (or 7) factors that increase the risk

cohort_answer.text: Considered HIGH RISK for transmission: Mother has acute or early untreated infection; Mother with viral load >1000 copies/mL within 4 weeks of delivery; Mother received no ART or less than 4 weeks of ART by time of delivery; little/no prenatal care especially at risk; Maternal immunologic status/WHO clinical stage (increased risk with CD4<200); Premature birth; Vaginal delivery among mothers with VL>1000; Heavy bleeding during delivery among those with detectable VL; Chorioamnionitis; Maternal mastitis

questions.question: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care

parts.text: What do you do for baby?

cohort_answer.text: At delivery: C/S prior to onset of rupture of membranes recommended; Intrapartum IV zidovudine; Avoidance of fetal scalp electrode monitoring; STAT HIV VL. Interventions on infant: LOW RISK: monotherapy PEP (4 weeks) with zidovudine; HIGH RISK: combination PEP (6 weeks) - 2 drug regimen AZT+3 doses NVP (resource-limited) or 3 drug regimen AZT, 3TC, treatment dose NVP (preferred). Advise against breastfeeding (developed countries). Test baby for HIV PCR at birth, 2 weeks, 1, 2, 4, 18 months

questions.question: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care. Baby tests HIV+ by PCR.

parts.text: Now what?

cohort_answer.text: Confirm HIV infection: positive PCR x2 prior to 18 months or reactive serology after 18 months. Continue 3-drug treatment regimen: Two NRTIs (AZT+3TC) + NVP, or Two NRTIs (AZT+3TC) + RAL (weight>2kg). Prevent opportunistic infection: start co-trimoxazole in infants (1st year of life) regardless of CD4 count (high risk PJP). Referral to pediatric HIV care provider

questions.question: Pregnant woman with CD4 550 and VL 20,000. Doesn't want treatment for herself.

parts.text: What 3 things can be done to decrease the risk of transmission to baby?

cohort_answer.text: C-section; Intra-partum prophylaxis with IV zidovudine; Post-partum prophylaxis; Avoid breastfeeding for the infant with zidovudine x6 weeks +/- nevirapine x1 week depending on maternal VL; Washing infant prior to Vitamin K injection

questions.question: Pregnant HIV+ woman declines treatment for herself.

parts.text: What 3 recommendations can you make to the OBGYN to decrease the risk of transmission to baby?

cohort_answer.text: C/S prior to rupture of membranes; Clean baby well prior to admin of vitamin K; Avoid artificial rupture of membranes; Avoid operative delivery with forceps or vacuum extractor; Avoid fetal scalp electrodes; Avoid breastfeeding

questions.question: HIV in pregnancy: MTCT. A pregnant woman HIV+ who is not currently treated (CD4 550, VL 1000) is having her second child. She took HAART during her first pregnancy and had a seronegative daughter. She does not want treatment for herself at this time.

parts.text: Suggest optimal pre-partum regimen
When would you treat?

cohort_answer.text: Intra-partum IV zidovudine during labor until delivery; Schedule C-section before rupture of membranes; Infant post-partum prophylaxis

questions.question: HIV+ woman at 34 weeks pregnancy

parts.text: Management

cohort_answer.text: Does she want treatment? Yes: Start ART right away with INSTI based regimen if able, IV zidovudine during labour. No: IV zidovudine during labour

questions.question: HIV+ woman at 34 weeks pregnancy

parts.text: Can she have a vaginal delivery?

cohort_answer.text: Depends on whether she is on ART and if VL<1000 copies. Ideally scheduled C/S at 38 weeks (if VL>1000, definitely needs C/S) prior to rupture of membranes

questions.question: A mother is found to be HIV+ at 16 weeks gestation. VL 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 410.

parts.text: Would you treat her?

cohort_answer.text: Yes

questions.question: A mother is found to be HIV+ at 16 weeks gestation. VL 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 410.

parts.text: If so, what meds and give your rationale?

cohort_answer.text: Refer to previous slide for regimen options (easiest to remember: Truvada and dolutegravir). Rationale: risk of vertical transmission without ANY treatment is 25-40%; risk drops to 1% when mothers prescribed ART >4 weeks before delivery

questions.question: A mother is found to be HIV+ at 16 weeks gestation. VL 16,000 copies/mL and CD4 410.

parts.text: What 2 recommendations should you make at the time of labor and delivery?

cohort_answer.text: IV zidovudine intrapartum from labor until delivery; Avoid fetal scalp monitors; C/S at 38 weeks before rupture of membranes if VL>1000 or unknown; No breastfeeding; Wash baby prior to giving IM vitamin K

questions.question: HCV and HIV mom at 18 weeks

parts.text: Need to quantify VL (PCR) at this point?

cohort_answer.text: Yes for HIV – need to know VL. For HCV – quantify at beginning of pre-natal care (also ALT), but not during it. Vertical transmission generally confined to women with detectable HCV RNA during pregnancy. HCV RNA levels rise during 1st and 3rd trimesters, peak in 3rd trimester, decrease postpartum. Try to treat HCV before pregnancy, avoid treating during pregnancy (drugs not tested in pregnancy)

questions.question: HCV and HIV mom at 18 weeks

parts.text: Is it safe to breastfeed?

cohort_answer.text: HIV – not safe. Hep C – available evidence suggests breastfeeding by an HCV-infected mother does not appreciably increase the risk of transmitting HCV

questions.question: HIV infected woman with second pregnancy. Not on HAART. Previous pregnancy bridged with HAART stopped postpartum. What to do now (2nd trimester)? CD4 450

parts.text: Recommended regimen
Why can you not use nelfinavir
Which drugs are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy?

cohort_answer.text: A) RAL or DRV/r or ATZ/r or DTG + ABC/3TC or TDF/3TC or TDF/FTC. B) Nelfinavir is a PI that should NOT be used in pregnancy due to low viral suppression. C) EVG/c combinations (low ARV levels during T2/T3); EFV controversial; DDI; D4T.

questions.question: HIV+ woman with second pregnancy, not on HAART, previous pregnancy bridged with HAART stopped post-partum. What to do now (2nd trimester)? CD4 450

parts.text: Why can you not use nelfinavir?

cohort_answer.text: Low drug concentrations in pregnancy, especially during the 3rd trimester and post-partum. Not shown to be teratogenic

questions.question: HIV+ woman with second pregnancy, not on HAART, previous pregnancy bridged with HAART stopped post-partum. What to do now (2nd trimester)? CD4 450

parts.text: What drug is absolutely contra-indicated in pregnancy?

questions.model_answer: Efavirenz is the ARV historically considered absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenicity/neural tube defect concern with first-trimester exposure), and should be avoided; restart ART now (2nd trimester) with a pregnancy-safe regimen (e.g. dolutegravir or raltegravir plus TDF/FTC) rather than resuming efavirenz-based therapy.

questions.question: HIV in newborn. You are consulted for a woman who was found to be HIV+ during delivery (already delivered).

parts.text: A) How would you care for the baby?

cohort_answer.text: No breastfeeding; Start baby on Zidovudine + Nevirapine + Lamivudine; Check HIV PCR at delivery and in 6 weeks; CBC+Diff, ALT, Cr, lactate; Hep B, C, syphilis serologies. HIV-1 PCR and serology within 48 hours of birth; additional PCR assays at 1 month or later; HIV serology at 18-24 months to document loss of transplacental maternal antibody

questions.question: HIV in the neonate: HIV+ mom presents at delivery with no antenatal care

parts.text: A) What is baby's risk of acquiring HIV?
B) List 4 (or 7) factors that increase risk
D) Baby tests HIV+ by PCR. Now what?
E) Treatment of Neonatal HIV

cohort_answer.text:
25% (in absence of ARV), reported rates 13-42%. With ARVs in labour, risk up to 10%
No ARV during pregnancy; Primary HIV infection (high viral load at seroconversion); High viral load >1000 at delivery; Low maternal CD4 count; Vaginal delivery; No intrapartum ARVs; Preterm delivery; Mom concurrent infections; STI; Chorioamnionitis
Repeat HIV PCR at 2 weeks to confirm; need 2 positive specimens from different draws to confirm; refer to pediatric HIV specialist; lifelong ARVs; check HIV antibody at 18 months
Zidovudine + Nevirapine + Lamivudine; Septra for 1st year of life; bloodwork monitoring (CBC, Cr, LFTs); vaccines (Hep B, meningococcal, pneumococcal, HiB, pneumococcal after 24 months, rotavirus if not severely immunocompromised, HPV/TDAP/MMR if CD4>200)

questions.question: A patient with HIV is pregnant. She is not on treatment:

parts.text: Name 3 antiretroviral regimens and when would you start them?
b. What 2 recommendations do you have for the mother at delivery?
c. What regimen for the baby and timing?
d. When would you test the baby?
e. 2 current Canadian recommendations for feeding?

cohort_answer.text: a) Dolutegravir/Abacavir/Lamivudine; TAF/Emtricitabine plus dolutegravir (or TDF); TAF/Emtricitabine plus Darunavir/ritonavir (or TDF, better studied). Start ASAP. b) VL>1000: C-section at 38 weeks and intrapartum zidovudine. VL<1000: delivery mode determined by OB, consider intrapartum zidovudine. Avoid artificial rupture of membranes, forceps/vacuum extractor, fetal scalp electrodes. c) Presumptive therapy at birth with Zidovudine, lamivudine + nevirapine or raltegravir. d) HIV NAT at birth and 6 weeks. e) Exclusive formula; no mixed feeding (solid/liquid foods prior to 6 months increases HIV transmission risk).

questions.question: 16 year old female with perinatally acquired HIV presents for routine follow up. She has positive syphilis serology with RPR 1:8 that was negative 6mo ago (Non-pregnant). She has no symptoms and exam is normal

parts.text: What stage of infection (0.5)
What treatment (drug, dose [Peds didn't ask dose], route, and duration) (0.5)
She is anaphylactic to penicillin. What alternative drug and duration can you use (did not ask dose) (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Stage: Early latent - asymptomatic with a negative test within 1 year (if no negative test within last year, automatically late latent). Treatment: 1x dose benzathine penicillin 2.4M units, given as 2x1.2M unit doses IM to each buttock. Alternatives: Doxy 100mg PO BID 10-14 days, ceftriaxone 1g IV/IM daily 10-14 days

questions.question: Infant just born one hour ago to a mother without antenatal care who was diagnosed with HIV and HBV during delivery

parts.text: Now what can be done for newborn to reduce HIV and HBV transmission (need two for each)

cohort_answer.text: HIV: No breastfeeding; Start triple therapy ZDV+NVP+3TC (ZDV 6 weeks, 3 doses NVP first week +/-3TC); HIV test at 6 weeks. HBV: Give HBIg within 12 hours of birth; give HBV vaccine now, at 1 month and 6 months

questions.question: HCV and HIV mom at 18 weeks

parts.text: Risk of transmission of HCV?

cohort_answer.text: Recent systematic review demonstrated a vertical transmission rate of 5.8% (95% CI 4.2-7.8) from HCV-infected mothers without HIV co-infection, and 10.8% (95% CI 7.6-15.2) with sub-optimally controlled HIV co-infection. ~10% in mothers with HIV and Hep C co-infection; 5-6% in mothers with Hep C mono-infection

questions.question: Woman with no antenatal care presents in labor, tests positive for HIV and Hepatitis B on rapid testing.

parts.text: 2 strategies to decrease risk of HBV transmission to baby

cohort_answer.text: IV zidovudine during labor until delivery; Elective CS recommended before rupture of membranes if VL unknown; Measure mom's VL and resistance testing; Avoid breastfeeding; Avoid fetal scalp monitoring
